newsitem.title: USA: Hilton seeks to compel ITT meeting in May.
newsitem.headline: Hilton seeks to compel ITT meeting in May.

text.p: Hilton Hotels Corp filed a motion for a preliminary injunction in a Nevada federal court seeking to compel ITT Corp to hold its annual meeting in May, a court clerk said on Thursday.
Court documents, filed late Wednesday in U.S. District Court in Las Vegas, cite ITT's own bylaws and case law as a legal basis for holding the meeting at its normal time.

ITT has in the past held its annual meeting in mid-May, but has not set a date for this year's shareholder conference. ITT officials have said recently that under Nevada state law, they are able to postpone the meeting until mid-November.

Hilton launched its $6.5 billion, or $55 a share, bid for ITT Corp on January 27. ITT rejected the offer, called it inadequate and told shareholders it would refocus on core businesses in hotels and gambling.
Hilton has vowed a proxy battle for control of ITT and on Monday, it began soliciting ITT shareholders for votes to elect Hilton's slate of directors at ITT's annual meeting.

In an affidavit filed with Hilton's motion, Daniel Burch, president of Hilton's proxy solicitation firm MacKenzie Partners Inc, asserted that if the meeting were held soon, ITT shareholders would favor the merger.

"I have little doubt that ITT's proxy solicitor has told the ITT board the same thing I have told my client:," Burch's affidavit said, "if the 1997 meeting were held today, there is a substantial likelihood that ITT shareholders would either vote the incumbent directors out of office or threaten to do so to induce them to negotiate with Hilton or another bidder."

In the motion, Hilton cites a 20-year history of ITT shareholder meetings in mid-May. Hilton claims because company by-laws are contracts between management and shareholders and because ITT's by-laws often use the term "annual meeting" a meeting postponement violate ITT's contract with stockholders.
Also, Hilton claims Nevada and federal case law has held that incumbent directors are unable to postpone a shareholder meeting and vote in order to avoid an electoral defeat.
Finally, Hilton argues that "no delay is needed" if ITT management claims it must postpone the meeting to implement its restructuring plan, which includes asset sales.
In its initial offer, Hilton also said it might monetize certain assets of ITT, excluding hotels and gambling units.
"The only difference between ITT's plan and Hilton's plan is that, under ITT's plan, an independent ITT remains under the control of incumbent management," the court papers said.
Hilton notes that by mid-May, ITT management will have had about four months to implement its plan, giving shareholders plenty of time to evaluate its direction.
"The shareholders are fully capable of deciding at a May annual meeting whether they want to permit the incumbent board to remain in control of their company," the court papers said.

Jim Gallagher, spokesman for ITT, called today's filing "old news" because Hilton addressed the issue of interfering with the board election process in an initial lawsuit filed in federal court in January.
U.S. District Judge Philip Pro, in whose court the case is being heard, set a March 5 hearing on the original Hilton motion. That hearing may now be delayed while the judge considers this new motion.
